evidence_quotes.quote: This study aims to identify illustrative cases that leveraged policy and systems change through existing policies and programs in communities to mitigate contaminants including lead, nitrates and arsenic to increase access to safe home drinking water from public or private sources.

This simultaneous, complementary mixed-methods (Dopp et al., 2019) study combined traditional legal and policy research, single-case study review methods, and economic evaluation using activity-based-costing and resource allocation from a societal perspective to create 5-year cost projections that compare strategies that can increase access to safe drinking water in homes of families with young children (i.e., aged 0–5 years). The economic evaluation is presented here. Additional research findings are available elsewhere.

Six case studies were completed, including three local and three statewide strategies (Table 1). The Northeast, Midwest, and West were represented, but the South was not. Two case studies were interventions within public water systems, and four were for private well owners. Two were initiated by policy changes, while others were programmatic efforts. Contaminants considered included nitrates, arsenic, and lead.

Key informants included water utility staff, state agency staff, a representative of a private company that contracts on safe water projects, researchers, and community organization staff. The research team interviewed 16 key informants (100 percent of those invited) using snowball sampling from a primary informant.

Researchers quantified the total numbers of households and eligible households with low income and young children, the numbers that would get information about their water quality, the proportion needing mitigation, and estimated the number of households that would adopt proven mitigation strategies, when needed, over 5 years using data derived from specific case research or from existing literature (Appendix A). Researchers estimated the 5-year total and average annual cost per household that gets information on water quality and per household adopting mitigation treatment.

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although framed around increasing equitable access to safe home drinking water, all six cases examine chemical contaminant testing and mitigation (lead, arsenic, and nitrates) in households that already have water supply—four involving private domestic wells and two involving already-connected public water systems (filter pitcher distribution in Denver and lead service line replacement in Cincinnati)—rather than household or community water or sanitation service access (connection, service availability, continuity, quantity, or utility service tariffs).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, this paper would satisfy Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it evaluates state, municipal, public utility, and WIC-administered policies and programs—including the New Jersey Private Well Testing Act (mandating well testing at property sale and every five years for rentals) and Cincinnati ordinances prohibiting private lead service lines with local financing/subsidies—even though the companion legal/policy analysis was published elsewhere (Wilking et al., 2022) and overall review decision under the plain reading still remains exclude due to C1 and C4. Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is not met (narrow = no): four of the six cases are programmatic clinical/WIC screening, provider training, education, and filter/bottled-water delivery initiatives (generic project delivery and behavioural promotion), none of the mechanisms directly govern water or sanitation service access (they govern water-quality testing and contaminant remediation), and this paper models them strictly as costed programmatic activity bundles rather than empirically evaluating a rule-type access mechanism.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Mixed-methods multiple single-case economic evaluation (activity-based micro-costing) drawing on 16 semi-structured key-informant interviews, program/utility/regulatory documents, American Housing Survey data, and WIC/SNAP administrative data to estimate resource use, costs, and 5-year projections across six US cases.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes are 5-year projected numbers of households receiving water-quality testing information, estimated proportions needing and adopting contaminant mitigation treatments (filter pitchers, point-of-use/point-of-entry filters, bottled water, or lead pipe replacement), and projected programmatic and household out-of-pocket contaminant-testing/remediation costs ($0.12 to $1,590 per household annually), rather than observed water or sanitation service access, connection, continuity, quantity, utility tariff affordability, or exclusion outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Unit of analysis (households, focusing on low-income households with young children aged 0-5 years), six state/local US case settings, interventions (six contaminant-testing and mitigation policies/programs), projected costing and uptake outcomes, and study design (activity-based micro-costing economic evaluation) are clearly identifiable in the text, even though Tables 1-4 are summarized in prose rather than rendered inline in the XML extract.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Mixed-methods multiple single-case economic evaluation (activity-based micro-costing with 5-year cost and reach projections supported by 16 semi-structured key-informant interviews and secondary/program data)
population_and_sample: Households (focusing on low-income families with young children aged 0-5 years) across six US case-study locations (New Jersey; New Hampshire and Vermont clinics; New Hampshire statewide WIC; Porterville, California; Cincinnati, Ohio; Denver, Colorado), informed by 16 key-informant interviews, program records, and American Housing Survey/WIC/SNAP data
exposure: Six state and local drinking-water contaminant testing and mitigation policies/programs (New Jersey Private Well Testing Act; NH/VT healthcare clinic arsenic well testing; New Hampshire WIC Water Well-Ness Initiative; Porterville CA nitrate testing, filter, and bottled-water program; Cincinnati Enhanced Lead Program; Denver Water Filter Program)
outcome: 5-year projected household reach of water-quality information, estimated adoption of contaminant mitigation strategies (62-80%), and projected total and average annual implementation and household out-of-pocket remediation costs by activity and payer
rationale: Excluded (E01 - Wrong topic): This study is an activity-based micro-costing economic evaluation projecting 5-year implementation costs and uptake of household drinking-water chemical contaminant testing and mitigation strategies (for lead, arsenic, and nitrates across four private-well cases and two already-connected municipal water systems). It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no), does not evaluate a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism directly governing service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope (c2 = no; companion legal/policy case work was published separately in Wilking et al., 2022), and reports projected contaminant-testing/mitigation reach and remediation costs rather than water/sanitation service access outcomes (c4 = no). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 it would pass c2 broadly, but still be excluded due to failing c1 and c4.
